extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying patent assignment and renewal law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing how assignments, reissues, renewals/extensions, and purchases interact with patent title and rights — who holds what after surrender/reissue or statutory extension, and how courts construe ambiguous statutory clauses about assignees' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of interests not in esse is not an assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract to convey a future interest in a term not yet obtained (interests not in esse at the time of the contract, e.g., renewals or extensions not yet obtained) has been held not to be an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to future interests deriving from renewals/extensions that the patentee had not yet obtained; an offer to perform a condition precedent before vesting does not convert the instrument into a grant. (Cases cited: Gibson v. Cook; Pitts v. Hall.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for assignment of patent applications (Gaylor v. Wilder)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a peculiar exception (illustrated by Gaylor v. Wilder) where a contract of assignment of a patent then applied for but not yet issued may be treated differently from ordinary future-interest contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise flags this as an exception to the general rule about future interests not in esse and advises not to overlook that case when dealing with assignments of pending applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of assignment during original term — vests indefeasible interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment made during and concerning the original term vests in the assignee an interest in the existing patent that is indefeasible by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reissue is treated as an amendment of the original patent from its commencement, an assignee's vested portion of the monopoly cannot be affected by the patentee's subsequent surrender and reissue without the assignee's consent. (Statutory background: surrender and reissue provisions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory surrender and reissue do not create new interests; assignees' rights protected
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute authorizing surrender and reissue (to correct a defective specification) is construed as amending the original patent rather than creating a new interest; existing assignments are not vacated by a surrender and reissue to the patentee alone — the reissued term enures to the assignee's benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where whole patent vested in assignee, assignee should make the surrender; where only part assigned, assignee should unite in surrender. If assignee consents to surrender, it becomes his act and he may be party in infringement suits. Therefore, it is not necessary to insert special protective clauses in assignments against reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special clause needed to protect assignee against reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect to reissues, it is not necessary to insert any special clause in an assignment to protect the assignee's interest, because the assignee's interest by operation of law remains the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains that reissue simply amends from commencement; prior assignments continue to enure to assignees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments under original term do not vest rights in extended term absent express conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee under the original term acquires no right under a subsequently extended (renewed) term unless such right is expressly conveyed to him by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the rule established by Mr. Justice Story and Mr. Justice McLean and upheld by subsequent courts: extensions are new grants and prior assignments generally do not carry forward the franchise to make and vend unless expressly provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of renewal clause protects users, not makers/vendors
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause that 'the benefit of such renewal shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented to the extent of their respective interests therein' is to be construed as saving the rights of those who were in the use of the patented article at the time of the renewal (purchasers/users), not as protecting prior assignees' exclusive rights to make and vend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority view (per opinion quoted) reasons that the statute's policy is to afford additional compensation to the patentee and to protect persons who had bought/use devices from being unjustly deprived by a late extension; to read the clause as conferring a full monopoly on prior assignees would subvert the statute's purpose. The clause in terms omits words necessary to create an exclusive right to make and vend, and thus must be read narrowly to protect merely the right to use the machine(s) in the hands of those using them at renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading ambiguous patent statutes according to legislative intent and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When words or phraseology of the statute are obscure or doubtful, the intention of the lawmakers, as discoverable from the context, general provisions, and policy of the patent law, should control the meaning; courts should avoid constructions that subvert the statute's object or produce harsh/unjust consequences absent very fixed and positive terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise quotes the Court's approach: prefer construction that reconciles doubtful language with the general policy (e.g., the eighteenth section's purpose of compensating the patentee) and avoid judicial creation of monopoly rights by strained interpretation of words like 'use.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh and fourteenth sections: assignments in writing, recording, and suits by assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent shall be assignable at law (as to whole interest or any undivided part) by an instrument in writing; such assignments/grants must be recorded in the Patent Office, and suits for infringement may be brought in the name of the assignee or grantee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions function to convert equitable interests into legal title so they can be enforced in law; this structural backdrop informs limits on the renewal clause and how contingent interests might be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent contractual interests looking to an extension are not created by renewal clause but may be converted to legal title after event
rubrics_metrics.description: A contingent interest in the new term derived from a provision in an assignment under the old term (looking to an extension) rests on contract and depends upon the contingency; the renewal clause does not 'create' such contingent interest but may change its character after the contingency occurs by making it a vested legal interest rather than merely contractual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains that any substantive right still depends on the contract between parties, but the clause may remove doubts about the legal nature of the contingent interest once the event happens; to that narrow extent the clause has effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchasers/users may continue to use and repair a specific patented machine after extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 guarantees that purchasers who were in the use of a patented machine at the time of renewal may continue to use the identical machine as long as it lasts and may repair it after an extension of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited establish that a purchaser who derived the right to use the machine from someone who could lawfully impart that right may continue to use and even repair the machine throughout the extended term; the clause protects these users against sudden deprivation by extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between franchise (make and vend) and mere right to use
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to make and vend the patented article is part of the franchise conferred by the patent and (absent stipulation) terminates in prior assignees at the end of the original term and becomes reinvested in the patentee upon extension; by contrast, the right to use the patented article (acquired by purchasers) takes the article out of the monopoly and makes it the purchaser's property for use/repair purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: prior assignees expecting to exercise the franchise in the extended term must obtain express conveyance or stipulation; purchasers may generally continue to use/repair articles they lawfully acquired and are in use at the time of renewal.
